title: Self-Supervised Pretraining of Molecular Graph Encoders with LeJEPA
summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its value for molecular graph neural networks remains contested. We ask whether pretraining on a large unlabelled corpus improves molecular property prediction. We adapt LeJEPA, a predictor-free joint-embedding predictive architecture regularised by Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularisation (SIGReg), to molecular graphs, evaluating GPS and Chemprop-style D-MPNN encoders on the Wong et al. [1] antibiotic-activity dataset and ogbg-molhiv using a multi-seed, bootstrap-based protocol. Pretraining improves learned representations but does not robustly improve finetuning. A frozen probe on pretrained embeddings exceeds random initialisation on both tasks (ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665; +0.123), reaching the published self-supervised band, but this does not translate into finetuning gains. On the antibiotic scaffold split, a canonical partition is significant (delta AUPRC +0.041, p = 0.010), but the effect vanishes across five partitions (pooled +0.013, p = 0.095). Finetuning is null on the random split, ogbg-molhiv, and D-MPNN. The representational edge is nevertheless recoverable. Embeddings saturate at ~16-32 effective dimensions, whereas Morgan fingerprints improve to 1024 bits. At matched dimensionality, fingerprints lead validation (0.799 vs 0.782 at 128 dimensions) but trail shifted test scaffolds (0.759 vs 0.788). Truncating embeddings and combining them with a 1024-bit Morgan fingerprint raises ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832 (delta +0.027; 95% CI [+0.003, +0.054]; p = 0.014); an untrained encoder gains nothing (delta -0.003). Thus, pretraining supplies complementary information best realised through feature-level combination, while finetuning gains are weak and partition-dependent.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether self-supervised pretraining on molecular graphs improves downstream property prediction. Using LeJEPA with SIGReg regularisation on GPS and D-MPNN encoders, the authors find pretraining improves frozen-probe representations (ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665 for random init) but does not robustly improve finetuning across most splits and models. The representational value is best harvested via feature-level combination: truncating pretrained embeddings and concatenating with 1024-bit Morgan fingerprints raises ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832, while an untrained encoder gains nothing.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its utility for molecular graph neural networks is unresolved; the authors aim to rigorously test whether pretraining on unlabelled molecular corpora translates into improved molecular property prediction.
AI.method: Adapts LeJEPA (a predictor-free joint-embedding predictive architecture regularised by Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularisation / SIGReg) to molecular graphs, using GPS and Chemprop-style D-MPNN encoders. Evaluates on the Wong et al. antibiotic-activity dataset and ogbg-molhiv with a multi-seed, bootstrap-based protocol, probing and finetuning, and comparing truncated embeddings combined with Morgan fingerprints.
AI.result: Frozen probes on pretrained embeddings beat random initialisation on both tasks (ogbg-molhiv +0.123), but finetuning gains are weak and largely non-significant—significant on one canonical antibiotic scaffold split (+0.041 AUPRC, p=0.010) yet vanishing across five partitions (p=0.095), and null on random splits, ogbg-molhiv, and D-MPNN. Embeddings saturate at ~16-32 dimensions vs 1024-bit fingerprints; at matched dimensions fingerprints lead validation but trail shifted scaffolds. Combining truncated embeddings with Morgan fingerprints improves ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832 (p=0.014); untrained encoders gain nothing.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining on molecular graphs provides complementary information best exploited through feature-level combination rather than finetuning, whose gains are weak and partition-dependent. The authors recommend re-evaluating how pretrained molecular representations are integrated into downstream tasks.

title: MarkerScout: A Disease-Agnostic Machine Learning Framework for Biomarker Prediction from Multi-Scale Mechanistic Models
summary:
We demonstrate the framework on three infectious diseases derived from a companion mechanistic immune-simulation platform: SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A Virus, and Plasmodium falciparum. Each disease was evaluated across hospitalization and intensive care unit cohorts, yielding six cohorts in total. Best-pipeline cross-validated macro F1 ranged from 0.82 for IAV-HOSP to 0.99 for COV-ICU, and the framework produced tiered, direction-aware biomarker lists for each disease and phase. Interleukin-18 (IL-18) reached the strongest tier in both SARS-CoV-2 phases with consistent direction.
  When benchmarked against three separate, independently collected clinical ICU datasets, MarkerScout's top-ranked features outperformed 94.4% of randomly selected feature sets of equivalent size for SARS-CoV-2, with a weaker but directionally consistent advantage for Influenza A Virus (66.7%) and Plasmodium falciparum (60.7%).

AI.tldr:
MarkerScout is a framework for identifying tiered, direction-aware biomarkers across multiple infectious diseases, applied to SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A Virus, and Plasmodium falciparum across hospitalization and ICU cohorts. It achieves cross-validated macro F1 scores from 0.82 to 0.99 and outperforms 94.4% of random feature sets on external ICU data for SARS-CoV-2.

The framework operates through a companion mechanistic immune-simulation platform, evaluating biomarkers across six cohorts (three diseases × two care settings). Key findings include IL-18 as a strong, consistently directed biomarker across both SARS-CoV-2 phases. External validation on independent clinical ICU datasets confirms the top-ranked features' superiority over random feature sets across all three diseases.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a robust framework (MarkerScout) for discovering and validating disease-specific biomarkers that are direction-aware (i.e., indicating whether a biomarker is up- or down-regulated) and tiered by importance, across multiple infectious diseases and clinical phases, with external validation against independent datasets to ensure generalizability.
AI.method: The framework integrates a mechanistic immune-simulation platform as the foundation, applies feature ranking/selections across six cohorts (three infectious diseases × two clinical settings: hospitalization and ICU), produces tiered biomarker lists with directional information per disease and phase, and validates top-ranked features on external independent ICU datasets by comparing their performance against randomly selected feature sets of equivalent size.
AI.result: Best-pipeline macro F1 ranges from 0.82 (IAV-HOSP) to 0.99 (COV-ICU). IL-18 achieves the strongest tier in both SARS-CoV-2 phases with consistent direction. External benchmarking shows top features outperform 94.4% of random feature sets for SARS-CoV-2, 66.7% for Influenza A Virus, and 60.7% for Plasmodium falciparum across independent ICU datasets.
AI.conclusion: MarkerScout provides a validated, generalizable biomarker discovery framework yielding strong classification performance and direction-aware biomarker insights across multiple infectious diseases, with the strongest and most consistent external generalization demonstrated for SARS-CoV-2.

title: Towards AI-Driven Nanomedicine Discovery: A Benchmark and Multimodal Learning Framework for Nano Self-Assembly Prediction
summary: Nano self-assembly organizes molecular components into bioactive nanoscale structures. Self-assembled nanoparticles (NAPs) derived from Chinese herbal formulas and applications such as anti-lung-cancer therapy demonstrate the substantial potential of self-assembly for nanomedicine discovery. Yet discovery still relies on costly wet-lab screening, while existing machine learning approaches lack standardized tasks, effective pairwise compatibility modeling, and public benchmarks with unified evaluation. To address these limitations, we formalize NSA prediction as a binary classification task for predicting self-assembly between molecular pairs and then establish NSA-Bench, the first public benchmark with curated molecular combinations, experimental conditions, self-assembly labels, and standardized evaluation protocols. We further develop NSA-Net, an interaction-aware multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular evidence from graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors to learn molecular-pair representations for self-assembly prediction. Extensive experiments on NSA-Bench show that NSA-Net achieves a ROC-AUC of $0.9470\pm0.0112$ (Small) and $0.9492\pm0.0062$ (Large). On the Small track, it surpasses the strongest machine-learning and graph-based baselines by 3.9 and 17.1 percentage points, respectively. Representation analyses reveal interpretable molecular characteristics associated with self-assembly prediction captured by the learned representations. Moreover, an NSA-Agent case study further demonstrates how NSA-Net predictions can support formulation refinement through experimental-condition-aware reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/developer-hq/NSA-Net.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NSA-Bench, the first public benchmark for nano self-assembly (NSA) prediction between molecular pairs, and NSA-Net, an interaction-aware multimodal framework integrating graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors. NSA-Net achieves ROC-AUC of 0.9470±0.0112 (Small) and 0.9492±0.0062 (Large), outperforming machine-learning and graph-based baselines by 3.9 and 17.1 percentage points respectively on the Small track.
AI.motivation: Nano self-assembly has great potential for nanomedicine discovery (e.g., anti-lung-cancer therapies from Chinese herbal formulas), but discovery relies on costly wet-lab screening. Existing machine learning approaches lack standardized tasks, effective pairwise compatibility modeling, and public benchmarks with unified evaluation.
AI.method: The authors formalize NSA prediction as a binary classification task predicting self-assembly between molecular pairs, establish NSA-Bench with curated molecular combinations, experimental conditions, labels, and standardized evaluation protocols, and develop NSA-Net—an interaction-aware multimodal framework that fuses graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors to learn molecular-pair representations.
AI.result: NSA-Net achieves ROC-AUC of 0.9470±0.0112 on Small and 0.9492±0.0062 on Large tracks, surpassing the strongest ML baselines by 3.9 percentage points and graph-based baselines by 17.1 percentage points on the Small track. Representation analyses reveal interpretable molecular characteristics, and an NSA-Agent case study demonstrates experimental-condition-aware reasoning for formulation refinement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and model advance nano self-assembly prediction by providing standardized evaluation and effective pairwise compatibility modeling, with potential to reduce reliance on costly wet-lab screening and support formulation optimization in nanomedicine discovery.

title: Advancing Alzheimer's Disease Treatment: Synergistic Ligand Combinations Targeting BACE1 via Multi-Ligand Simultaneous Docking
comment: \c{opyright} 2025 by the Author(s). This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License
summary: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioral changes, primarily affecting the elderly. Current treatments focus on symptom management as no therapies effectively halt or reverse disease progression. Newer therapies targeting BACE1, a key enzyme in amyloid plaque formation, have shown promise in clinical trials, though they have been limited by side effects and insufficient efficacy in slowing cognitive decline. This is the first study where multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) was employed to identify potential synergistic inhibitor combinations from among thousands of small molecules that could yield better results than the current phase-III inhibitors of BACE1. The recent phase III drugs such as Atabecestat, Elenbecestat, Lanabecestat, and Verubecestat were considered to be standards for comparison in this study. A library of small molecules with known IC50 values against BACE1 was filtered for flagging Pan-Assay Interference (PAINS) and "Brenk" compounds. Single-ligand docking revealed individual ligand interactions with the protein, forming the basis for creating ligand pairs tested in MLSD. Among these combinations, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3656158, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3695732, Verubecestat and CHEMBL3656158, and CHEMBL4078427 and Lanabecestat demonstrated excellent binding affinity of -19.90 kcal/mol, -18.45 kcal/mol, -18.07 kcal/mol, and -17.67 kcal/mol with the protein, which is significantly greater than those of phase-III inhibitors, along with inter-ligand interactions indicative of a synergistic effect. These findings underscore the transformative potential of MLSD in identifying synergistic compound interactions, paving the way for novel combination therapies in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

AI.tldr: This study applies multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) to identify synergistic inhibitor combinations for BACE1, an enzyme central to Alzheimer's disease pathology. Screening thousands of small molecules against phase-III inhibitors (Atabecestat, Elenbecestat, Lanabecestat, Verubecestat), the authors identified four ligand pairs with superior binding affinities and inter-ligand interactions, suggesting synergistic effects that could outperform current single-drug therapies.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no curative therapies. While BACE1 inhibitors (targeting amyloid plaque formation) have advanced to phase-III trials, they suffer from side effects and insufficient efficacy in slowing cognitive decline. The authors aim to discover synergistic multi-drug combinations that outperform existing single phase-III inhibitors.
AI.method: The study employs multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD), a computational technique allowing multiple ligands to dock simultaneously. A small-molecule library with known IC50 values for BACE1 was filtered to remove PAINS and Brenk flagged compounds. Single-ligand docking established individual ligand interactions, which informed the construction of ligand pairs subsequently tested via MLSD. Binding affinities were compared against four phase-III BACE1 inhibitors as standards.
AI.result: Four ligand pairs demonstrated superior binding affinities relative to phase-III inhibitors: CHEMBL4078427 + CHEMBL3656158 (-19.90 kcal/mol), CHEMBL4078427 + CHEMBL3695732 (-18.45 kcal/mol), Verubecestat + CHEMBL3656158 (-18.07 kcal/mol), and CHEMBL4078427 + Lanabecestat (-17.67 kcal/mol). Inter-ligand interactions indicated synergistic effects within these combinations.
AI.conclusion: MLSD shows transformative potential for identifying synergistic compound interactions in BACE1 inhibition. The identified ligand pairs may pave the way for novel combination therapies in Alzheimer's disease treatment, offering a promising alternative to current single-drug phase-III inhibitors that exhibit insufficient efficacy and side effects.

title: A Roadmap for MEG Foundation Models
summary: Foundation models are beginning to reshape brain-signal analysis by moving the field beyond task-specific decoding pipelines toward reusable models pretrained on broad neural datasets. Magnetoencephalography (MEG) is a compelling but still underdeveloped target for this shift: it captures human cortical dynamics at millisecond resolution while offering stronger spatial interpretability than EEG, making it especially valuable for source-resolved studies of perception, language, cognition, and clinical brain function. Yet MEG foundation models remain at an early stage, with only a small number of MEG-specific and MEG-inclusive multi-modal models, modest pretraining corpora, and emerging but still limited benchmarks. This perspective lays down the basic concepts needed to understand MEG foundation models and provides a didactic overview of the field's key design choices, including tokenization, sensor- versus source-space representations, sensor-geometry encoding, backbone architectures, self-supervised objectives, and pretraining data. We then offer a roadmap for future development, organized around native MEG pretraining, adaptation of EEG foundation models, transfer from generic time-series models, and multi-modal integration with EEG, fMRI, MRI, behaviour, and stimulus features. We highlight the need for coordinated infrastructure, including diverse and reusable MEG datasets, rigorous evaluation across subjects, sites, tasks, and clinical settings, and responsible data-sharing practices that address consent, privacy, access, and governance.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper discusses the emerging field of Magnetoencephalography (MEG) foundation models, which aim to move brain-signal analysis beyond task-specific pipelines toward reusable models pretrained on broad neural datasets. It provides a didactic overview of key design choices (tokenization, sensor/source space, geometry encoding, architectures, objectives, data) and offers a roadmap for future development including native MEG pretraining, EEG foundation model adaptation, transfer from generic time-series models, and multi-modal integration. The paper also emphasizes the need for coordinated infrastructure, rigorous benchmarks, and responsible data governance.
AI.motivation: MEG captures human cortical dynamics at millisecond resolution with better spatial interpretability than EEG, making it valuable for source-resolved studies of perception, language, cognition, and clinical function. However, MEG foundation models remain at an early stage with few models, modest pretraining corpora, and limited benchmarks, motivating this perspective to lay out concepts and a development roadmap.
AI.method: The paper is a perspective/review that (1) establishes foundational concepts for understanding MEG foundation models, (2) provides a didactic overview of key design choices including tokenization, sensor- vs source-space representations, sensor-geometry encoding, backbone architectures, self-supervised objectives, and pretraining data, and (3) outlines a roadmap organized around native MEG pretraining, EEG foundation model adaptation, generic time-series transfer, and multi-modal integration.
AI.result: The paper identifies the current state of MEG foundation models as nascent, surveys the design space and trade-offs in building them, and proposes a structured roadmap for advancing the field alongside necessary infrastructure requirements (diverse/reusable datasets, rigorous cross-subject/site/task evaluation, and responsible data-sharing practices).
AI.conclusion: Advancing MEG foundation models requires coordinated community efforts spanning model design, dataset curation, evaluation standardization, and ethical data governance. Native MEG pretraining, transfer from existing EEG foundation models, and multi-modal integration each offer complementary paths forward that together could unlock MEG's full potential for brain-signal research and clinical applications.

title: The physical foundation beneath protein generative modeling
summary: Physical equations in protein modeling appear to have been replaced by generative models trained directly on structure data. By learning a mapping from noise to data, sampling de novo protein structures has become much more efficient. However, such models can also learn non-physical features and break down with out-of-distribution settings which are typical in protein design campaigns. In this review, we highlight where the physics persists in protein generative modeling pipelines and the issues that linger when physically relevant components of a macromolecular system are left unmodeled. We present a perspective that respecting the underlying physics of macromolecular systems, increasingly through learned representations that are physically grounded and updating generative models with experimental data, is foundational to generative modeling for functional protein design.

AI.tldr: This review argues that while generative models have replaced explicit physical equations in protein design, physics still plays a crucial role. The authors contend that physically grounded learned representations and integration of experimental data are foundational for functional protein design, as purely data-driven models can learn non-physical features and fail in out-of-distribution settings.
AI.motivation: Generative models trained directly on structure data have made de novo protein sampling efficient, but they can learn non-physical features and break down in out-of-distribution settings typical of protein design campaigns. The paper aims to highlight where physics persists in these pipelines and what issues arise when physically relevant components are unmodeled.
AI.method: This is a perspective/review paper that surveys where physics remains embedded in protein generative modeling pipelines, examines failure modes when physics is ignored, and proposes that physically grounded learned representations combined with experimental data updating are essential directions forward.
AI.result: The paper identifies gaps in current generative protein models due to unmodeled physical components and advocates for integrating physics through grounded representations and experimental feedback to enable robust functional protein design.
AI.conclusion: Respecting underlying macromolecular physics—increasingly via physically grounded learned representations and experimental data updating—is foundational for generative modeling aimed at functional protein design.

title: When Quantization Breaks Memory: Recurrent-State Write-Back in Low-Precision Temporal Inference
summary: Quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory demands of neural-network inference. In recurrent networks, however, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, so the rule used to store that state can alter subsequent computations. Here, we introduce recurrent-state write-back to denote this rule and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder--decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, a molecular imaging modality used in quantitative biological imaging. A central task is estimating two lifetime parameters, the short-lived component τ1 and the long-lived component τ2, from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. Holding the trained model fixed, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by approximately 70x and 300x, respectively. Failure occurs when repeated small updates remain below the write threshold, leaving the stored state nearly fixed while the network continues to propose change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory carry information from these suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps show that increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training shows that compatibility with the state interface can be learned. To test whether this behavior extends beyond the GRU, we repeat the post-training intervention in an independently trained LSTM, where coarse write-back reproduces the failure, error feedback restores accuracy, and state-specific interventions reveal greater sensitivity of the cell state than the hidden state. Our results establish recurrent-state write-back as a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics and identify the state-storage interface as a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "recurrent-state write-back" as the rule governing how quantized recurrent network states are stored and returned across time steps. Using a GRU encoder-decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, the authors show that deterministic 4-bit state storage causes ~70x and ~300x increases in estimation errors for τ1 and τ2. They demonstrate that error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory can recover accuracy without retraining, and verify the phenomenon generalizes to LSTM architectures.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces compute/memory costs of neural networks, but in recurrent networks the quantized state persists and affects future computations. The authors identify that the specific rule for storing recurrent state (write-back) is underexplored and can dramatically affect performance, which matters for deploying quantized recurrent models in applications like fluorescence lifetime imaging.
AI.method: The authors define recurrent-state write-back and isolate its effect by holding a trained GRU encoder-decoder fixed and replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic low-precision (4-bit) state storage. They analyze failure mechanisms (repeated sub-threshold updates leaving state frozen), propose interventions (error feedback, residual memory, direction memory), perform precision sweeps, and validate findings with matched training and independent LSTM experiments.
AI.result: Deterministic 4-bit state storage increases τ1 and τ2 estimation errors by ~70x and ~300x respectively. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory recover accuracy without retraining. Increasing state precision can worsen fixed recurrent solutions, but matched training can learn compatibility. The same failure pattern and recovery via error feedback are reproduced in an independently trained LSTM, where the cell state shows greater sensitivity than the hidden state.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent-state write-back is a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics. The state-storage interface (how quantized states are stored and fed back) should be a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference systems.

title: A Semantic Model of Genetic Evidence: A Step Toward Bridging the Basic-Science-Clinic Gap
comment: 16 pages; supplementary material (32 pages) included in this submission. Schema, annotations, and code: https://github.com/ForomePlatform/genetic-evidence-model (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22260686)
summary: Scientific and clinical decision-making depends on evidence from the primary literature, but existing standards for representing that evidence (FHIR Evidence, ECO, SEPIO, and the GA4GH Genomic Knowledge Standards) are oriented toward clinical-trial workflows, evidence codes, or single-variant assertions, and do not capture the fine-grained, domain-specific structure of claims in basic and pre-clinical research. We introduce a semantic model for scientific evidence with three core classes, specialize it for genetics, align it structurally to FHIR Evidence with a SEPIO-anchored credibility decomposition, and attach a compact dimensional vocabulary whose conditional-activation rules are validated by a SHACL schema for the implemented constraints. Using clinical variant interpretation as the driving use case, we evaluate the model through a human-AI annotation pilot over six genetics papers, yielding 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions, with a workflow that keeps curator-authored reference annotations distinct from AI-drafted annotations. Treating the pilot as a feasibility study rather than a benchmark, we argue that the model is a useful increment toward trustworthy, AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation: a reference data model and validation schema for representing genetic evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a semantic model for scientific evidence in basic and pre-clinical research, specialized for genetics and structurally aligned with FHIR Evidence and SEPIO standards. A pilot study with human-AI annotation over six genetics papers yielded 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions, demonstrating the model as a feasible increment toward trustworthy, AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation.
AI.motivation: Existing evidence representation standards (FHIR Evidence, ECO, SEPIO, GA4GH Genomic Knowledge Standards) focus on clinical-trial workflows, evidence codes, or single-variant assertions, failing to capture the fine-grained, domain-specific structure of claims in basic and pre-clinical genetics research, which is essential for scientific and clinical decision-making.
AI.method: The authors design a semantic model with three core classes, specialize it for genetics, align it structurally to FHIR Evidence with a SEPIO-anchored credibility decomposition, and attach a compact dimensional vocabulary whose conditional-activation rules are validated by a SHACL schema. They evaluate the model through a human-AI annotation pilot over six genetics papers, keeping curator-authored reference annotations distinct from AI-drafted annotations.
AI.result: The pilot yielded 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions from six genetics papers, with a workflow separating curator reference annotations from AI drafts. The results support the model's usefulness as a feasibility study rather than a formal benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The model represents a useful increment toward trustworthy, AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation by providing a reference data model and validation schema for representing genetic evidence from basic and pre-clinical research.

title: Stochastic epidemic models with pulse vaccination, varying infectivity and waning immunity
summary: We introduce a fully stochastic, non-Markovian SIRS-type epidemic model that incorporates varying infectivity, waning immunity and a pulse vaccination strategy that may not confer permanent immunity. The model is constructed at the individual level, where each person is characterized by random infectivity and susceptibility functions, and vaccination campaigns occur at the jump times of a Poisson random measure with arbitrary intensity. We rigorously derive the epidemic dynamics as the large-population limit of an interacting stochastic particle system, leading to a system of nonlinear Volterra-type integral equations governing the average susceptibility and total force of infection. We establish a functional law of large numbers(FLLN) for the empirical processes and provide explicit expressions for the limiting compartmental proportions. The long-term behavior of the system is analyzed: we prove that the infection-free solution is globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number falls below a critical threshold, and that the disease persists when this threshold is exceeded. The threshold is given by the harmonic mean of the maximal susceptibility across individuals and generalizes previous results by incorporating vaccination and memory effects. Our framework provides a probabilistically grounded extension of classical deterministic pulse vaccination models and offers new insights into the control of epidemics through scheduled immunization policies.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a fully stochastic, non-Markovian SIRS-type epidemic model with varying infectivity, waning immunity, and pulse vaccination with non-permanent immunity. The authors derive the large-population limit of an interacting particle system, obtaining nonlinear Volterra integral equations, establish a functional law of large numbers, and analyze long-term disease dynamics including global stability of the infection-free state and disease persistence based on a generalized basic reproduction number threshold.
AI.motivation: Classical deterministic pulse vaccination models lack probabilistic grounding and cannot adequately capture individual-level heterogeneity in infectivity, susceptibility, waning immunity, and finite-duration vaccine protection. A rigorous stochastic framework at the individual level is needed to provide more realistic epidemic modeling and insights into scheduled immunization policies.
AI.method: The model is built at the individual level with random infectivity and susceptibility functions, with vaccination events occurring at jump times of a Poisson random measure with arbitrary intensity. The authors take the large-population limit of an interacting stochastic particle system, rigorously deriving mean-field dynamics as a system of nonlinear Volterra-type integral equations. They establish a functional law of large numbers for empirical processes and analyze the long-term dynamics through stability analysis of the infection-free equilibrium and disease persistence conditions.
AI.result: The authors prove the infection-free solution is globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number is below a critical threshold, and disease persists when the threshold is exceeded. The reproduction number threshold is expressed via the harmonic mean of maximal susceptibility across individuals, generalizing prior results by incorporating vaccination and memory (non-Markovian) effects.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a probabilistically rigorous extension of classical deterministic pulse vaccination models, offering improved understanding and tools for controlling epidemics through scheduled immunization policies in realistic heterogeneous populations.

title: VizIt: A multi-view framework for exploring single-cell, spatial, and genetic data online
summary: Multi-omic studies increasingly require data to be examined from complementary biological perspectives, yet interactive exploration remains fragmented across modalities and tools. We present VizIt, an open-source framework for multi-view exploration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic, epigenomic and genetic data. VizIt connects gene-, cell type-, condition-, spatial-, genomic region- and variant-centered views, enabling seamless navigation across biological perspectives. We demonstrate VizIt through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas, a customizable interactive multi-omic resource.

AI.tldr: VizIt is an open-source framework for interactive multi-view exploration of multi-omic data, connecting gene-, cell type-, condition-, spatial-, genomic region-, and variant-centered views, demonstrated through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas.
AI.motivation: Multi-omic studies generate data that needs to be examined from complementary biological perspectives, but interactive exploration remains fragmented across different modalities and tools, preventing seamless navigation.
AI.method: VizIt is an open-source framework that integrates six complementary views (gene-, cell type-, condition-, spatial-, genomic region-, and variant-centered views) to enable seamless navigation across single-cell and spatial transcriptomic, epigenomic, and genetic data.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas, a customizable interactive multi-omic resource.
AI.conclusion: VizIt provides a unified framework for multi-view exploration of heterogeneous omic data, addressing the fragmentation of interactive tools across biological perspectives.

title: Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty
summary: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

AI.tldr: SUDO (Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport) is a framework for solving unbalanced dynamic optimal transport with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties, overcoming limitations of existing solvers that are restricted to quadratic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao penalties or require expensive NeuralODE simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing UDOT solvers are either computationally expensive (relying on NeuralODE simulations) or restricted to quadratic growth penalties (WFR geodesics). This limits the ability to encode general biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis when inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots.
AI.method: SUDO learns conditional paths and transport costs, solves an induced semi-coupling problem, and leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. The authors first demonstrate that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport separate, then design SUDO for general non-quadratic convex growth penalties.
AI.result: On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient analytical solution-driven algorithms while being faster than simulation-based methods. For non-WFR settings, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties encoding proliferation-dominant priors, producing more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.
AI.conclusion: SUDO provides an efficient, simulation-free framework for UDOT with general convex growth penalties, expanding beyond the quadratic penalty limitation and enabling more flexible biological priors for cellular dynamics inference.

title: Eco-evolutionary cycles in a matching type predator-prey interaction
summary: We study the population dynamics of a predator-prey system with two types in each species. Within a species, predator or prey, dynamics are described by a neutral competitive Lotka-Volterra model, i.e., birth, death and competition parameters are equal for both types. Additionally, we assume that the intra- and inter-type competition parameters are equal. The predator-prey interaction is defined by a matching-types model where predators of type $i$ exclusively interact with prey of type $i$. The individual-based model is described by a birth-death process with immigration, where immigration reflects mutations between the types of the same species. We completely describe the deterministic dynamics arising as a large population limit of this birth-death process. We find that depending on the parameters, potential equilibria are the coexistence of all four types, coexistence of a non-matching or matching pair of predators and prey, or the extinction of the predator or prey species resulting in a line of two-type equilibria. When mutations are sufficiently rare, then the predator-prey dynamics are described by successive jumps between the different deterministic equilibria on this mutational time scale. These jumps describe eco-evolutionary cycles of repeated prey or predator invasions and declines. When coexistence of all the types is possible, we show that these cycles accumulate on this time scale. Lastly, to prove that after the accumulation point the system converges to the coexistence equilibrium, we consider a slightly modified model with unequal intra- and inter-type competition parameters. This modified setting allows us to conclude that after the accumulation point all four populations remain macroscopic and converge to the coexistence equilibrium.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the population dynamics of a predator-prey system with two types per species, modeled by a neutral competitive Lotka-Volterra framework with matching-type interactions and rare mutations. The authors fully characterize deterministic large-population limits—which include coexistence equilibria, matching/non-matching pair equilibria, and extinction lines—and show that rare mutations drive eco-evolutionary cycles between equilibria that may accumulate, after which the system converges to a coexistence equilibrium (proven via a modified model).
AI.motivation: The goal is to understand how neutral diversity within predator and prey species interacts with selective predator-prey dynamics under mutation, particularly how eco-evolutionary dynamics unfold across multiple timescales when mutations are rare.
AI.method: The individual-based model is a birth-death process with immigration (representing mutations). The authors derive the deterministic limit for large populations and analyze potential equilibria. For the rare-mutation regime, they study successive jumps between equilibria on the mutational timescale and examine cycle accumulation. A modified model with unequal intra- and inter-type competition is used to prove post-accumulation convergence to coexistence.
AI.result: Potential equilibria include coexistence of all four types, coexistence of matching or non-matching predator-prey pairs, or extinction of one species leaving a line of two-type equilibria. Rare mutations produce eco-evolutionary cycles of repeated prey/predator invasions and declines. When full coexistence is possible, cycles accumulate on the mutational timescale, and after this point all four populations remain macroscopic and converge to the coexistence equilibrium (confirmed in the modified model).
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a complete characterization of the deterministic dynamics and rare-mutation eco-evolutionary behavior, demonstrating that cycles can accumulate and lead to stable coexistence when mutations are sufficiently frequent relative to the evolutionary timescale.

title: A Short Combinatorial Proof of the Pons-Batle Identity for Counting Tree-Child Networks
summary: Tree-child networks are a useful class of binary phylogenetic networks. The Pons--Batle identity (Pons and Batle, \textit{Scientific Reports}, 2021) states that the number $a_{n,k}$ of tree-child networks with $k$ reticulations on $n$ taxa satisfies \[ a_{n,k}=(n-k+1)a_{n,k-1} +\frac{n(2n+k-3)}{n-k}a_{n-1,k}. \] In this paper, we present a short combinatorial proof of this identity.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a short combinatorial proof of the Pons–Batle identity, a recurrence relation that counts tree-child networks with a given number of taxa and reticulations.
AI.motivation: The Pons–Batle identity is a useful recurrence for counting tree-child networks, but the original proof was likely analytic or computational in nature. The authors aim to give a purely combinatorial explanation for why the identity holds.
AI.method: The authors present a short combinatorial proof demonstrating that the number a_{n,k} of tree-child networks with k reticulations on n taxa satisfies the given recurrence relation.
AI.result: A concise combinatorial proof of the Pons–Batle identity is established.
AI.conclusion: The Pons–Batle identity is validated through a simple combinatorial argument, providing clearer insight into the structure of tree-child networks.

title: Layered mixed matrices and reaction networks
summary:
The purpose of this work is twofold. In the first part, we consider layered mixed matrices introduced by Murota, relate them to existing notions in combinatorial commutative algebra, and investigate the irreducibility of their determinants. Furthermore, for a layered mixed matrix in combinatorial canonical form, we determine the sparsity structure of its inverse. That is, we characterize which entries of the inverse are nonzero.
  In the second part, we establish for the first time a formal connection between these algebraic results and the theory of buffering structures for reaction networks developed by Mochizuki and Okada. We identify the lattice of buffering structures with the lattice of order ideals of the block poset of the combinatorial canonical form of the associated layered mixed matrix. This allows us to characterize the reducibility of the symbolic Jacobian determinant as a polynomial in the reaction-rate derivatives, as well as the nonzero sensitivity responses of species concentrations to reaction-rate perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a formal connection between layered mixed matrices (from combinatorial commutative algebra) and buffering structures in reaction networks. It characterizes the irreducibility and inverse sparsity of layered mixed matrices, and links the lattice of buffering structures to order ideals of the block poset of the combinatorial canonical form, enabling characterization of symbolic Jacobian determinant reducibility and sensitivity responses in reaction networks.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bridge two previously disconnected areas: algebraic results on layered mixed matrices (introduced by Murota) and the theory of buffering structures for reaction networks developed by Mochizuki and Okada. This is the first formal connection between these algebraic and biological/network-theoretic frameworks.
AI.method: The work proceeds in two parts: (1) analyzing layered mixed matrices by relating them to combinatorial commutative algebra notions and investigating determinant irreducibility and inverse sparsity structure under combinatorial canonical form; (2) formally linking these results to buffering structures by identifying the lattice of buffering structures with the lattice of order ideals of the block poset associated with the combinatorial canonical form of the layered mixed matrix.
AI.result: The authors characterize which entries of the inverse of a layered mixed matrix in combinatorial canonical form are nonzero, determine the irreducibility of determinants, and characterize (a) the reducibility of the symbolic Jacobian determinant as a polynomial in reaction-rate derivatives, and (b) the nonzero sensitivity responses of species concentrations to reaction-rate perturbations in reaction networks.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a novel formal bridge between combinatorial algebra (layered mixed matrices) and reaction network theory (buffering structures), showing that algebraic properties of layered mixed matrices directly translate to structural characterizations of reaction network sensitivities and Jacobian determinant reducibility.

title: Quantum Optimisation for Protein-Protein Interaction Network Alignment
summary: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network alignment combines topological and sequence information to identify conserved modules across species, but global alignment remains challenging: heuristics sacrifice optimality, while exact methods lack scalability. We model the alignment as a weighted maximum common induced subgraph problem and reformulate it through the modular product graph to a minimum-weight vertex cover on the complement, with node weights carrying sequence similarity. To solve this problem, we develop a hybrid framework combining kernelisation, branch-and-bound, and seven Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) formulations. These formulations differ in how the cover constraints are enforced, from penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian to mixers confined to the feasible subspace. For single round QAOA, we derive closed-form expressions for the expected cost of four circulant mixer variants, enabling performance characterisation without circuit simulation. Applied to synthetic and real-world networks reduced to KEGG pathways, the QAOA formulations achieve high topological conservation on the aligned core while at least maintaining biological conservation comparable to leading classical aligners, at the cost of reduced node coverage. Across selected KEGG pathways, the aligned subnetworks retain disease-associated proteins, preserving biologically relevant information. Cheaper formulations leave more edges uncovered, while enforcing feasibility in the mixer raises circuit depth by one to two orders of magnitude. Together, these results highlight the potential of quantum optimisation for PPI network alignment and the resource trade-offs that will shape its scalability as quantum hardware matures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical framework for global protein-protein interaction (PPI) network alignment, formulated as a weighted maximum common induced subgraph problem solved via minimum-weight vertex cover on the modular product graph complement. Seven QAOA formulations with varying constraint enforcement strategies are developed and benchmarked against classical aligners, showing competitive topological/biological conservation but reduced node coverage, with feasibility-enforcing mixers incurring significantly higher circuit depth.
AI.motivation: Global PPI network alignment is important for identifying conserved functional modules across species, yet existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off: heuristic methods sacrifice solution optimality, while exact methods cannot scale to real biological networks. This motivates exploring alternative solution paradigms, particularly quantum optimisation, to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The alignment problem is modelled as a weighted maximum common induced subgraph (wMCIS) problem, reformulated via the modular product graph into a minimum-weight vertex cover (MWVC) formulation on the complement, with node weights encoding sequence similarity. A hybrid solver combines kernelisation, branch-and-bound, and seven QAOA variants that differ in how vertex cover constraints are enforced—from penalty-based cost Hamiltonians to mixers restricted to the feasible subspace. Closed-form expected cost expressions are derived for four circulant mixer variants for single-round QAOA, avoiding costly circuit simulation.
AI.result: On synthetic and real KEGG pathway networks, the QAOA formulations achieve high topological conservation on the aligned core with biological conservation comparable to leading classical aligners, though at the cost of reduced node coverage. Aligned subnetworks retain disease-associated proteins. Cheaper constraint formulations sacrifice edge coverage, whereas feasibility-enforcing mixers increase circuit depth by one to two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Quantum optimisation shows genuine promise for PPI network alignment, achieving competitive conservation quality, but scalability will depend on resolving resource trade-offs—notably the balance between formulation cost and circuit depth—as quantum hardware matures.

title: A Generalizable Feature Extractor for Alzheimer's-Related Brain MRI Tasks
comment: 26 pages (excluding the references section), 7 figures (excluding sub-figures)
summary: When there is not enough labeled data to properly train deep learning models, transfer learning can help. We still do not fully understand how effective it is in neuroimaging, especially for Alzheimer's disease research. It is also not clear if these transferred models can work on new datasets without being retrained for each specific task. We evaluate whether a compact, supervised pretrained model can serve as a reusable foundation model for downstream neuroimaging tasks. We freeze the 7.18 million weights of a 3D CNN previously trained for brain-age prediction, and adapt it to each task using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. We evaluate generalizability in six experiments. Adapting the model to classify cognitively normal versus Dementia on ADNI gave an AUC of 0.964 on held-out folds (Experiment #1). Applying that adapted model unchanged to OASIS-3, with no retraining, gave an AUC of 0.871 (Experiment #2). Reusing its output logit together with age and a cognitive score distinguished stable from progressing MCI with an AUC of 0.828 (Experiment #3). Adapting the same backbone to predict amyloid positivity from structural MRI gave an AUC of 0.804 (Experiment #4). Finally, the same approach estimated ICV-normalized hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes directly from the T1w image, with R^2 of 0.80 and 0.91 respectively, tasks normally addressed with much larger U-Net networks (Experiments #5 and #6). A compact model supervised on brain age can therefore serve as a reusable backbone, adapting to each task with ~1% additional parameters and transferring to an unseen cohort without any training. Our findings suggest that a carefully trained brain age model can serve as an effective foundation model for Alzheimer's related tasks, even under strict data constraints.

AI.tldr: A compact 3D CNN pretrained for brain-age prediction serves as a reusable foundation model for neuroimaging tasks. Using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with only ~1% additional trainable parameters, the frozen backbone generalizes across six Alzheimer's-related experiments, including classification, disease progression, amyloid positivity prediction, and volumetric estimation, with strong performance on both seen and unseen cohorts.
AI.motivation: There is insufficient labeled data in neuroimaging (particularly Alzheimer's research) to train deep learning models from scratch, and it is unclear whether transfer learning—specifically pretrained models—can generalize to new datasets without per-task retraining.
AI.method: The authors freeze a 3D CNN (7.18M weights) previously trained for brain-age prediction and adapt it to downstream tasks using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. The adapted model is evaluated across six experiments: dementia classification on ADNI, cross-cohort transfer to OASIS-3 without retraining, MCI progression prediction with auxiliary clinical features, amyloid positivity prediction from structural MRI, and estimation of hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes.
AI.result: The model achieved an AUC of 0.964 for dementia classification on ADNI, 0.871 when applied unchanged to OASIS-3, 0.828 for MCI progression, 0.804 for amyloid positivity, and R² values of 0.80 and 0.91 for hippocampal volume and white matter hypointensity estimation respectively—performance comparable to much larger U-Net architectures.
AI.conclusion: A compact model supervised on brain age can serve as an effective and reusable foundation model for Alzheimer's-related tasks, adapting with minimal parameters and transferring to unseen cohorts without retraining, even under strict data constraints.
